To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the chemical composition of a surface can be determined from the ratio of core-shell ionization cross-sections of the elements, measured in a reflection experiment, if the relative cross-sections for transmission geometry are known.

the chemical composition of an oxide surface can be determined by reflection electron energy loss spectroscopy (REEL) if (1) the surface is clean and free from contamination, (2) the surface has the correct stoichiometry, and (3) the experimental geometry is carefully chosen.

the development of the quantitative analysis of surfaces using the REELS technique.
the development of a quantitative surface microanalysis technique for the study of the surface and interfacial properties of solids.
the development of a new surface microanalysis method, based on the reflection electron energy-loss spectrometer, for quantitative chemical analysis of surfaces.

, for quantitative surface micro-analysis by REELS, the following conditions should be satisfied: 1) The specimen surface is atomically clean and well ordered; 2) The electron beam is normal to the sample surface; 3) The electron beam energy is in the range of 100 to 500 eV; 4) The collection semi-angle is 03B2 1 mrad; and 5) The EICS is known to within ± 20% accuracy.
the surface composition of a MgO thin film is determined with an accuracy of 15%.

REELS is capable of quantitative surface chemical analysis, but only under the conditions of (1) high energy resolution, (2) small collection semi-angle, (3) small scattering angle, and (4) the use of the relative EICS measured from thin foil specimens.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the EICS is the key to the quantitative surface microanalysis of solids using REELS.
the REELS method is an effective and powerful technique for quantitative surface analysis, and the experimental conditions for obtaining the high quality core-shell edges are well defined.
the REELS technique is a powerful tool for quantitative surface chemical analysis.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the EICS is a function of both the collection semi-angle and the resonance diffraction condition, and that the EICS can vary by a factor of 3-10 from the value measured under the specular "mirror" reflection condition.
the surface chemical composition is determined by the ratio of the EICS for the surface and bulk atoms, which is not a constant.
the REELS technique is a powerful tool for surface microanalysis of insulators, but that the EICS must be determined accurately for the particular experimental conditions of the REELS measurement.
